name: libnl
why: A library for Linux netlink, the kernel's internal messaging channel for networking, a real door into protocols most people never see.

brief.what_it_is: libnl is a suite of C libraries that give programs access to Linux netlink, the kernel's messaging interface used mainly for networking configuration and monitoring. The suite is split into small libraries: libnl (core socket handling, message construction, parsing, send and receive), libnl-route (network interfaces, routes, addresses, neighbours, traffic control), libnl-genl (generic netlink), and libnl-nf (netfilter conntrack, log, and queue). The repository file listing also shows libnl-xfrm, libnl-idiag, and libnl-cli, plus a python directory. Programs call its APIs and get kernel networking state back or change it.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs describe netlink as a more flexible successor to ioctl for networking-related kernel configuration and monitoring. The docs also say the interfaces are split into several small libraries so applications do not have to link against one bloated library.
brief.how_it_works: Applications open netlink sockets, build messages, and send them to kernel subsystems, then parse the replies. Each protocol family (route, generic netlink, netfilter) gets its own library on top of the core. The docs call netlink an IPC mechanism primarily between the kernel and user space processes.
brief.install_notes: The docs recommend installing from your Linux distribution's packages first and list package names per distro, for example libnl-3-dev on Debian and Ubuntu, libnl3-devel on Fedora and openSUSE, and libnl-devel on CentOS. The repo tree includes autogen.sh and configure.ac, which suggests a standard autotools build from source, but I did not see build commands in any page I read. The stated requirement is Linux, since netlink is a Linux kernel interface.
brief.standout: It is a plain C library that talks directly to kernel networking subsystems over netlink, which most people never touch. Its split-by-protocol design lets an application link only the family it needs.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub page shows 2,213 commits, 491 stars, and a .github/workflows directory, but I did not see a last-commit or release date. The docs site names 3.2.25, released Jul 16, 2014, as the latest stable release, which suggests the release line may be quiet, though the git repo may still see commits.
brief.caveats: The GitHub homepage fetch returned the LGPL-2.1 license text instead of a README, so I have no README content and no README commands. Most of the description comes from the external docs site at infradead.org. The license is LGPL-2.1. The docs site lists 3.2.25 from 2014 as latest stable. Its Known Bugs section says releases 3.2.18 and 3.2.19 shipped with an incorrect SONAME, and that 3.2.18 and 3.2.19 binaries need relinking against 3.2.20 and later. The 1.1.x series has limited support and the docs say not to develop new applications on libnl1.

It was designed to be a more flexible successor to ioctl to provide mainly networking related kernel configuration and monitoring interfaces.
The interfaces are split into several small libraries to not force applications to link against a single, bloated library.
